prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a single clean idea, magic-wavelength trapping that cancels the light shift of the clock transition while holding many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, with an experimental programme that has been independently reproduced in strontium, ytterbium and other species at several national laboratories. Fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, routine intercontinental comparisons, relativistic geodesy, tighter limits on drifting constants and a credible path to a redefinition of the second give it breadth beyond one subfield. It is also the candidate in which the opening ballots converge most strongly: four first places, five top-three rankings and all eight members ranking it. The two-name credit is compact and fits the invention (Katori) and the record performance and many-body clock physics (Ye). I would present it as a prize for a new measurement regime rather than an incremental successor to the comb and ion-clock prizes.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and boundary: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb on which these clocks rely and the 2012 prize covered single-ion control, so a third clock-related prize invites the charge that the area is already recognised and that lattice clocks are a refinement of that tradition. Credit is also not airtight, since Lemonde, Hollberg, Sterr and the ion-clock groups made real contributions, and the formal redefinition of the second has not yet happened. I think the first concern is answered by the physics, because the many-atom magic-wavelength scheme reaches a different stability and systematics regime than a single ion, but the committee should state that argument explicitly in the citation rather than assume it.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B003) first as a clear, original discovery of new phases that has spawned a large independent field, and ripe after about seven years of replication.
responses.response: I agree that B003 is original and has had striking impact, and it is my first alternative. My reservation is the one you partly acknowledge: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled and several correlated phases depend on twist-angle disorder and sample quality. A prize shortly after the dust has settled is safer than one while the central interpretive question remains open. By contrast the lattice-clock performance is quantitative and has been checked by independent clock comparisons, so I would not treat the two as equally mature. I also doubt the credit is complete, since you note yourself that the first experimental author is absent from the names.

responses.point: Mehlig places active matter and flocking (B006) first as a conceptually clear statistical-physics advance, Vicsek's transition plus Toner-Tu long-range order in two dimensions, and judges the recognition timely.
responses.response: This is outside my field, so I am wary of arguing the physics against you. The Toner-Tu result that order survives in two dimensions is a deep point, and I take it seriously. What gives me pause is your own admission that quantitative confirmation of the scaling exponents is incomplete and that the field may be seen as biology-facing. Opening ballots show only you ranking it first and no one else ranking it highly, so I would like to hear from the other theorists whether the experimental tests of the exponents are good enough. I would not move it ahead of a result whose predictions are measured to many digits, but I do not want to dismiss it as a matter of taste.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks Car-Parrinello ab initio molecular dynamics (B058) first for its four decades of impact, clean two-person attribution, and overdue recognition, while noting the question of method versus discovery.
responses.response: The attribution is the cleanest on the list and I do not dispute the lasting impact. My difficulty is the committee's own criteria: B058 is a computational method whose consequences lie largely in chemistry and materials simulation, and the 1998 prize for density-functional theory already covers the foundation. I would support it only if we are prepared to say that a simulation algorithm is a physics invention in the same sense as a new instrument or measurement scheme. If the committee believes that, B058 deserves to be taken as seriously as the clock. Only two members ranked it at all, so I would put it behind the candidates with broader support.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks Katori and Ye first, stressing the AC Stark shift cancellation and many-body systematics as core atomic physics, and calls the work a clean, timely successor to the 2005 prize.
responses.response: I share your assessment and want to make one point sharper. You describe it as a successor to the comb prize, and I think that framing is a risk, since a sceptic will read 'successor' as 'incremental'. I would rather defend it as the realisation of a different idea, many neutral atoms interrogated in a state-insensitive trap, which the comb alone could not supply. Your point that the credit leaves out Lemonde, Sterr and Hollberg is a fair qualification, and I think it should be handled in the citation wording rather than by enlarging the prize beyond Katori and Ye.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the comb (2005) and ion-clock (2012) prizes, and how the citation should say so.
Whether the missing formal redefinition of the second counts against recognition now or is irrelevant to the discovery.
Whether Lemonde, Hollberg, Sterr or the ion-clock leaders have a claim strong enough to change the credited pair; the supplied credit does not resolve this.
Whether B003 will look more mature once the pairing mechanism is better understood; I cannot assess that from the evidence given.
statement.conflict_note: Potential connection: during my doctoral period I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's frequency-comb prize is part of the boundary argument for this candidate. I also work in laser spectroscopy and coherent light-matter interactions, the tradition in which these clocks sit, and I have taken part in WACQT. Beyond this field proximity, no personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile, but the committee may wish to consider whether the Hall connection requires recusal on the clock discussion.
